{{for|continuous images of separable complete metric spaces, known as Lusin spaces|Polish space #Lusin spaces}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Luzin space''' (or '''Lusin space'''), named for [[Nikolai Luzin|N. N. Luzin]], is an [[uncountable]] topological [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> space]] without [[isolated point]]s in which every [[nowhere-dense]] subset is [[countable]]. There are many minor variations of this definition in use: the T<sub>1</sub> condition can be replaced by [[Separation axiom#Main definitions|T<sub>2</sub> or T<sub>3</sub>]], and some authors allow a countable or even arbitrary number of isolated points.

The existence of a Luzin space is independent of the axioms of [[ZFC]]. {{harvtxt|Lusin|1914}} showed that the [[continuum hypothesis]] implies that a Luzin space exists. 
{{harvtxt|Kunen|1977}} showed that assuming [[Martin's axiom]] and the negation of the [[continuum hypothesis]], there are no [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] Luzin spaces.

== In real analysis ==

In [[real analysis]] and [[descriptive set theory]], a '''Luzin set''' (or '''Lusin set'''), is defined as an uncountable subset {{mvar|A}} of the [[real numbers|reals]] <math>\R</math> such that every uncountable subset of {{mvar|A}} is [[nonmeager]] (that is, of the second Baire category) in <math>\R.</math>
Equivalently, {{mvar|A}} is an uncountable subset of <math>\R</math> that meets every [[meager subset]] of <math>\R</math> (i.e., first category set) in only countably many points.
Equivalently, {{mvar|A}} is an uncountable subset of <math>\R</math> that meets every [[nowhere dense]] subset of <math>\R</math> (i.e., first category set) in only countably many points.

Luzin proved that, if the continuum hypothesis holds, then every nonmeager set in <math>\R</math> has a Luzin [[subset]]. Obvious properties of a Luzin set are that it must be nonmeager (otherwise the set itself is an uncountable [[meagre set|meager subset]]) and of [[measure zero]], because every set of positive measure contains a meager set that also has positive measure, and is therefore uncountable.

A '''weakly Luzin set''' is an uncountable subset of a real [[vector space]] such that for any uncountable subset the set of directions between different elements of the subset is dense in the sphere of directions.

The [[measure-category duality]] provides a [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] analogue of Luzin sets – sets of positive [[outer measure]], every uncountable subset of which has positive outer measure.  These sets are called [[Sierpiński set]]s, after [[Wacław Sierpiński]]. Sierpiński sets are weakly Luzin sets but are not Luzin sets.

==Example of a Luzin set==

Choose a collection of 2<sup>ℵ<sub>0</sub></sup> meager subsets of '''R''' such that every meager subset is contained in one of them. By the continuum hypothesis, it is possible to enumerate them as ''S''<sub>''α''</sub> for countable ordinals ''α''. For each countable ordinal ''β'' choose a real number ''x''<sub>''β''</sub> that is not in any of the sets ''S''<sub>''α''</sub> for ''α''<''β'', which is possible as the union of these sets is meager so is not the whole of '''R'''. Then the uncountable set ''X'' of all these real numbers ''x''<sub>''β''</sub> has only a countable number of elements in each set ''S''<sub>''α''</sub>, so is a Luzin set.

More complicated variations of this construction produce examples of Luzin sets that are [[subgroup]]s, [[field extension|subfield]]s or [[real closed field|real-closed subfield]]s of the real numbers.
